edition.copy_text: Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI

source_text: Ὅρα δὴ ἐντεῦθεν ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς πῶς τὴν καὶ παρ᾿ Ἑλλήνων τισὶν οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτως φιλοσοφήσασιν εἰσαγομένην τοῦ κόσμου ἐκπύρωσιν μετὰ χλεύης διαβάλλων θέλει ἡμᾶς ὡσπερεὶ μάγειρον ποιοῦντας τὸν θεὸν εἰσάγειν τὰ περὶ τῆς ἐκπυρώσεως· οὐ συνιδὼν ὅτι, ὥσπερ Ἑλλήνων τισὶν ἔδοξε (τάχα παρὰ τοῦ ἀρχαιοτάτου ἔθνους Ἑβραίων λαβοῦσι), τὸ πῦρ καθάρσιον ἐπάγεται τῷ κόσμῳ εἰκὸς δ᾿ ὅτι καὶ ἑκάστῳ τῶν δεομένων τῆς διὰ τοῦ πυρὸς δίκης ἅμα καὶ ἰατρείας· καίοντος μὲν καὶ οὐ κατακαίοντος τοὺς μὴ ἔχοντας ὕλην δεομένην ἀναλοῦσθαι ὑπ᾿ ἐκείνου τοῦ πυρὸς, καίοντος δὲ καὶ κατακαίοντος τοὺς ἐν τῇ διὰ τῶν πράξεων καὶ λόγων καὶ νοημάτων τροπικῶς λεγομένῃ οἰκοδομῇ „ξύλα, χόρτον ἢ καλάμην“ οἰκοδομήσαντας. φασὶ δ᾿ οἱ θεῖοι λόγοι τὸν κύριον „ὡς πῦρ χωνευτηρίου καὶ ὡς ποίαν πλυνόντων“ ἑκάστῳ τῶν δεομένων ἐπιδημήσειν διὰ τὸ ἀναμεμῖχθαι οἱονεὶ φαύλην χυτὴν ὕλην τὴν ἀπὸ τῆς κακίας, δεομένων δὲ λέγω πυρὸς, οἱονεὶ χωνεύοντος τοὺς ἀναμεμιγμένους „χαλκῷ“ „καὶ κασσιτέρῳ καὶ μολίβδῳ.“ καὶ ταῦτα τὸν βουλόμενον ἔστιν ἀπὸ τοῦ προφήτου Ἰεζεκιὴλ μαθεῖν. ὅτι δὲ οὐχ ὡς μάγειρόν φαμεν τὸ πῦρ ἐπιφέρειν τὸν θεὸν ἀλλ᾿ ὡς θεὸν εὐεργέτην τῶν χρῃζόντων πόνου καὶ πυρὸς, μαρτυρήσει καὶ ὁ προφήτης ῾Πσαΐας ἐν ᾧ γέγραπται λελέχθαι πρός τι ἔθνος ἁμαρτωλόν· „ὅτι ἔχεις ἄνθρακας πυρὸς, καθίσαι ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς· οὗτοι ἔσονταί σοι βοήθεια.“ οἰκονομούμενος δ᾿ ὁ λόγος ἁρμόζοντα πλήθεσιν ἐντευξομένοις τῇ γραφῇ ἐπικεκρυμμένως μετὰ σοφίας λέγει τὰ σκυθρωπὰ εἰς φόβον τῶν μὴ δυναμένων ἄλλως ἐπιστρέψειν ἀπὸ τῆς χύσεως τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων· πλὴν καὶ οὕτως ὁ τηρῶν εὑρήσει ἐμφαινόμενον τὸ ἀπὸ τῶν σκυθρωπῶν καὶ ἐπιπόνων ἐπαγόμενον τοῖς ἀλγοῦσι τέλος. ἀρκεῖ δ᾿ ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος παραθέσθαι ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἡσαΐου τό· „ἕνεκεν τοῦ ἐμοῦ ὀνόματος δείξω σοι τὸν θυμόν μου, καὶ τὰ ἔνδοξά μου ἐπάξω ἐπὶ σὲ, ἵνα μὴ ἐξολοθρεύσω σε.“ ἠναγκάσθημεν δὲ τὰ μὴ ἁρμόζοντα τοῖς ἁπλούστερον πιστεύουσι καὶ δεομένοις τῆς ἁπλουστέρας ἐν λόγοις οἰκονομίας αἰνίξασθαι, ἵνα μὴ δοκῶμεν ἀνεξέλεγκτον ἐᾶν τὴν τοῦ Κέλσου κατηγορίαν, λέγοντος· ἐπειδὰν ὁ θεὸς ὥσπερ μάγειρος ἐπενέγκῃ τὸ πῦρ.
thought_title: The fire that cleanses and heals
pass_a_gloss: See then (ὅρα δή) from the beginning how, slandering (διαβάλλων) with mockery (χλεύης) the conflagration (ἐκπύρωσιν) of the world introduced also by some of the Greeks who philosophised not contemptibly (οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτως), he wishes us, as if making God a cook, to introduce the things about the conflagration; not perceiving (συνιδών) that, as seemed good to some Greeks (perhaps taking it from the most ancient nation of the Hebrews), the fire is brought on the world as purifying (καθάρσιον), and likely (εἰκός) also on each of those needing the penalty (δίκης) and at once healing (ἰατρείας) through the fire; burning (καίοντος) and not burning up (κατακαίοντος) those not having matter (ὕλην) needing to be consumed (ἀναλοῦσθαι) by that fire, but burning and burning up those who in the building (οἰκοδομῇ) figuratively (τροπικῶς) spoken of, through deeds, words and thoughts (νοημάτων), have built 'wood, grass (χόρτον) or straw (καλάμην)'. The divine words say the Lord 'as fire of a smelting furnace (χωνευτηρίου) and as soap (ποίαν) of washers (πλυνόντων)' will visit (ἐπιδημήσειν) each of those needing, because of there being mixed in (ἀναμεμῖχθαι) as it were base (φαύλην) fusible (χυτήν) matter, that from wickedness (κακίας); those needing fire I mean, as it were smelting (χωνεύοντος) those mixed with 'bronze and tin and lead'. And these things whoever wishes can learn from the prophet Ezekiel. That we say God brings on the fire not as a cook but as God, benefactor (εὐεργέτην) of those needing toil (πόνου) and fire, the prophet Isaiah also will witness, in whom it is written to have been said to a certain sinful nation: 'Since you have coals of fire, sit on them; these will be a help (βοήθεια) to you.' The Word, managing (οἰκονομούμενος) things fitting for multitudes who will come upon (ἐντευξομένοις) the Scripture, speaks the gloomy things (σκυθρωπά) hiddenly (ἐπικεκρυμμένως) with wisdom, for fear of those unable otherwise to turn back from the outpouring (χύσεως) of sins; yet even so the one observing (τηρῶν) will find shown forth the end (τέλος) brought on by the gloomy and toilsome things for those in pain (ἀλγοῦσι). It suffices for the present to set beside from Isaiah: 'For the sake of my name I will show you my wrath (θυμόν), and my glorious things (ἔνδοξα) I will bring upon you, that I may not utterly destroy (ἐξολοθρεύσω) you.' We were compelled (ἠναγκάσθημεν) to hint (αἰνίξασθαι) at things not fitting for those believing more simply (ἁπλούστερον) and needing the simpler economy (οἰκονομίας) in words, that we may not seem to leave unrefuted (ἀνεξέλεγκτον) the accusation (κατηγορίαν) of Celsus, saying: when God like a cook brings on the fire.

choices.why: ἐντεῦθεν: now rendered ('See, then, how here, from the very start')
ὥσπερ Ἑλλήνων τισὶν ἔδοξε: removed added 'also'
ὕλη, matching 'the matter that comes from wickedness'
οἰκονομούμενος ... ἐντευξομένοις τῇ γραφῇ: calque 'meet with Scripture' changed to 'read Scripture'; 'ordering' to 'arranging'
τῶν μὴ δυναμένων (present): 'could not' changed to 'cannot'
ἐμφαινόμενον: 'made plain' (too strong beside 'veiled') changed to 'shown there'

pass_b_english: See, then, how here, from the very start, he slanders with mockery the burning of the world, a teaching put forward also by some Greeks whose philosophy is not to be despised, and how he would have it that we, as though making God a cook, bring in our account of that burning. He has not seen that, as some Greeks held (perhaps having taken it from the most ancient nation, the Hebrews), the fire is brought upon the world to cleanse it, and probably also upon each of those who need the punishment and at the same time the healing that comes through fire. It burns, but does not burn up, those who have no matter that needs to be consumed by that fire; but it burns and burns up those who, in the building that is spoken of figuratively, the building of deeds, words and thoughts, have built with “wood, hay or straw” (1 Corinthians 3:12).

The divine words say that the Lord will come “like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ soap” (Malachi 3:2) to each of those who need it, because there has been mixed into them, as it were, a base matter that melts, the matter that comes from wickedness; to those, I mean, who need fire, as though he were smelting those who have been mixed with “bronze and tin and lead” (Ezekiel 22:18–20). Anyone who wishes may learn this from the prophet Ezekiel.

That we do not say God brings the fire like a cook, but as God, the benefactor of those who need pain and fire, the prophet Isaiah will also bear witness, in the place where it is written that it was said to a certain sinful nation: “Since you have coals of fire, sit upon them; these will be a help to you” (Isaiah 47:14–15). The Word, arranging what suits the multitudes who will read Scripture, speaks the grim things in a veiled way and with wisdom, to bring fear on those who cannot otherwise turn back from the flood of their sins. Even so, the attentive reader will find shown there the end that the grim and painful things bring about for those who suffer. For the present it is enough to set down these words from Isaiah: “For my name’s sake I will show you my anger, and I will bring my glories upon you, so that I may not utterly destroy you” (Isaiah 48:9).

We have been compelled to hint at things that do not suit those who believe more simply and who need a simpler handling in our teaching, so as not to seem to leave unrefuted the charge Celsus makes when he says, “when God, like a cook, brings on the fire.”
notes: ἐκπύρωσις = the Stoic doctrine of the world's periodic conflagration, rendered 'the burning of the world'. The source prints ῾Πσαΐας, a misprint for Ἡσαΐας (Isaiah). ὡς ποίαν πλυνόντων: the LXX of Malachi 3:2 has πόα ('fullers' herb', i.e. soap). The Ezekiel reference is to the smelting of Israel mixed with bronze, tin and lead (Ezekiel 22:18–20 LXX; LXX lists bronze, iron, tin, lead); same numbering in English. Isaiah 47:14–15 follows the LXX, which has the coals as a help; the Hebrew says there is no coal to warm oneself by. Isaiah 48:9 LXX ('I will bring my glories upon you') differs from the Hebrew ('for my praise I restrain it for you'). χύσις τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων ('outpouring of sins') rendered 'flood of their sins'. The closing quotation repeats Celsus's words from 5.14. Isaiah 47:14-15: in Rahlfs the coals clause ends 47:14 and 'these will be a help to you' opens 47:15.
